nameStory: Morrow's honeysuckle gets its name from Dr. James Morrow, a ship's surgeon who served as botanist on Commodore Matthew Perry's expedition to Japan in the 1850s. He collected many plant specimens during this historic mission that opened Japan to Western trade. The "honeysuckle" part comes from the sweet nectar that can be sipped from the flowers, just like our native species.
description: Morrow's honeysuckle is a deciduous shrub that typically grows 6-10 feet tall and wide, forming dense thickets over time. This non-native invader from East Asia has an upright, spreading growth habit with arching branches that create a somewhat rounded shape. In late spring, it produces pairs of small white or cream-colored tubular flowers that age to yellow, followed by bright red berries in summer. Despite its pretty appearance, this aggressive spreader crowds out native plants in forests and edges.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval leaves arranged in opposite pairs along the stem, each 1-3 inches long with smooth edges and a soft, slightly fuzzy texture underneath. The leaves have prominent veining and feel somewhat thick between your fingers.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small tubular flowers appear in pairs at leaf joints, starting white or cream and aging to yellow. Each flower is about half an inch long and smells sweetly fragrant, especially in the evening.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Bright red berries appear in pairs in mid-summer, each about 1/4 inch across. The berries are translucent when ripe and contain several small seeds, but taste bitter unlike the sweet flowers.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms dense, spreading shrubs with multiple upright to arching stems from the base. Older specimens create impenetrable thickets as branches layer and root where they touch the ground.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Mature stems have light brown bark that peels in long, papery strips, revealing lighter brown underneath. Young twigs are smooth and often reddish-brown in color.

habitat: Morrow's honeysuckle thrives in forest edges, old fields, roadsides, and disturbed areas throughout New England. It tolerates a wide range of soil conditions from dry to moist, and grows in both full sun and partial shade. You'll often find it invading the understory of deciduous and mixed forests, especially where there's been some disturbance.

seasonality.spring: Leaves emerge early in spring before most native shrubs, giving it a competitive advantage. The distinctive paired white flowers bloom in late May to early June, creating a sweet fragrance in the evening air.
seasonality.summer: Bright red berries ripen in pairs by mid-summer and persist into fall, making this the easiest season for identification. The dense green foliage remains healthy-looking even during drought.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn yellow-green to yellow before dropping, but the bright red berries remain prominent and are attractive to birds. Fall color is generally unremarkable compared to native shrubs.
seasonality.winter: The papery, peeling bark on older stems becomes very noticeable, and you can often find dried berry remnants still clinging to branches. The multiple-stemmed growth pattern is clearly visible.

funFact: Morrow's honeysuckle is such an effective invader that it can completely change forest soil chemistry - its leaf litter decomposes differently than native plants, creating conditions that favor more invasive species and make it harder for native wildflowers to return even after the honeysuckle is removed.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other invasive bush honeysuckles like Tatarian and Amur honeysuckle, which also have opposite leaves and red berries in pairs. The key difference is that Morrow's honeysuckle flowers are white aging to yellow, while Tatarian's are pink to red and Amur's stay white. Remember: "Morrow's goes mellow yellow."
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "bush honeysuckle," this invasive species shouldn't be confused with our beneficial native honeysuckles like coral honeysuckle, which is a vine with orange-red flowers. The name "bush honeysuckle" is commonly applied to several invasive Asian honeysuckle species that have become major ecological problems in North America.
compareHints: Unlike native fly honeysuckles which have flowers in clusters and blue or black berries, Morrow's honeysuckle has flowers and berries strictly in pairs with red fruit. It's much more aggressive and forms denser thickets than native species. Compared to Japanese honeysuckle (a climbing vine), Morrow's grows as an upright shrub and has much less fragrant flowers.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike the invasive Japanese, Morrow's, and Tatarian honeysuckles that dominate many New England areas, American fly-honeysuckle has distinctively paired berries and a much more restrained growth habit.
Japanese honeysuckle is unique among New England honeysuckles for its white-to-yellow color change and semi-evergreen leaves.
Unlike native American fly-honeysuckle which stays small and has paired flowers on long stalks, Amur honeysuckle grows into a large shrub with flowers sitting directly on the branches.
Among New England honeysuckles, coral honeysuckle is the only one with scentless, coral-red tubular flowers and that distinctive leaf-fusion around the stem.
Among New England's honeysuckles, glaucous honeysuckle is the only climbing species with that distinctive waxy blue-green leaf coating and cup-forming fused upper leaves.
Unlike our native fly honeysuckles which have flowers in clusters and blue or black berries, Tatarian honeysuckle always has paired flowers and red berries.
Mountain fly-honeysuckle differs from American fly honeysuckle by having much fuzzier leaves and preferring higher elevation habitats.
Among New England's honeysuckles, the dense coating of soft hairs immediately separates this species from smooth-leaved Japanese honeysuckle or the only slightly hairy American fly honeysuckle.
Fly honeysuckle stands out from other honeysuckles in New England by its paired red berries and shrubby growth habit - most others either climb like vines or have different colored berries.
Unlike the vigorous vining Japanese honeysuckle, winter honeysuckle is a well-behaved shrub that doesn't climb.
Unlike the more common American fly honeysuckle which prefers drier woods, swamp fly honeysuckle demands wet feet and boggy conditions.

Unlike the ubiquitous Japanese honeysuckle which blooms white to yellow and has simple opposite leaves, common honeysuckle has those distinctive fused upper leaves and more intensely fragrant flowers.
While New England has many honeysuckle species, perfoliate honeysuckle is the only one with fused upper leaves that the stem appears to grow through.
Unlike the invasive Asian honeysuckles that plague New England (Japanese, Morrow's, Amur), twinberry honeysuckle doesn't spread aggressively and has the unique twin-berry-in-red-bracts feature.
Unlike the aggressive Japanese honeysuckle that stays white then turns yellow, grape honeysuckle flowers age to pink.
Unlike its weedy relatives like Japanese honeysuckle (which climbs) or Morrow's honeysuckle (which has red berries), sweetberry honeysuckle stays compact and produces edible blue fruit.
